key_concept: The shape of a species follows from its electron pairs around the central atom (VSEPR, $sp^3$, $sp^3d$, $sp^3d^2$), while for a complex like $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ it follows from the hybridisation set by the strong-field ligand ($dsp^2$).
steps: A. $PCl_5$: P has 5 valence electrons and forms 5 P–Cl bonds with 0 lone pairs. That is 5 bond pairs, $sp^3d$ hybridisation, so the shape is trigonal bipyramidal (III).

B. $BrF_5$: Br has 7 valence electrons. Five go into Br–F bonds, leaving 1 lone pair. That is 6 electron pairs (5 bp + 1 lp), $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation. The electron geometry is octahedral, and with one position taken by the lone pair the shape is square pyramidal (IV).
C. $BF_4^-$: B has 3 valence electrons, plus 1 from the negative charge, giving 4. These form 4 B–F bonds with 0 lone pairs, $sp^3$ hybridisation, so the shape is tetrahedral (I).

D. $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$: Ni is in the $+2$ state, which is $3d^8$. $CN^-$ is a strong-field ligand, so the 8 d-electrons pair up in four 3d orbitals and leave one 3d orbital empty. Hybridisation is $dsp^2$, so the shape is square planar (II), and the complex is diamagnetic.
Matching: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II, which is option (2).
why_not_others: Option (1) gives $PCl_5$ a square pyramidal shape, but it has no lone pair, so it must be trigonal bipyramidal. Options (3) and (4) make $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ square pyramidal, which is impossible for a 4-coordinate species; (3) also wrongly makes $BrF_5$ tetrahedral and $BF_4^-$ square planar, and (4) wrongly makes $BrF_5$ square planar.
common_trap: Students often apply a simple 4-pairs-means-tetrahedral rule to $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ and forget that strong-field $CN^-$ forces $dsp^2$ (square planar), unlike $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$, which is $sp^3$ and tetrahedral.
time_saving_tip: Fix the two sure matches first: $PCl_5$ is trigonal bipyramidal (III), which eliminates option (1), and $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ is square planar (II), which eliminates (3) and (4). Only option (2) remains.
